title: Regions, monuments and wine
subtitle: Je suis allé dans le Bordelais. Quelle merveille !
summary: Talk about a holiday in the French regions: villages, historic monuments, wine and the expressions people use to say how much they enjoyed it.

lesson.heading: Telling a friend about your trip
lesson.text: Antoine is back from a weekend near Bordeaux, and his friend wants to hear everything. Notice how he describes where he went, when he arrived and what he brought back. These past forms with **je suis ...** are explained in the grammar lesson; here, just learn them as phrases.

examples.text: *Étienne :* **Où est-ce que tu es allé**, finalement ?
examples.note: So where did you go in the end?

examples.text: *Antoine :* **Je suis allé** dans le Bordelais. Je suis arrivé juste à la fin des **vendanges**.
examples.note: I went to the Bordeaux region. I arrived just at the end of the grape harvest.

examples.text: Je suis revenu avec **une caisse de** pomerol.
examples.note: I came back with a case of Pomerol (a Bordeaux wine).

examples.text: Je me suis ruiné, mais **tant pis** !
examples.note: I spent a fortune, but never mind!

examples.text: La vieille ville **date du XVIIIe siècle**.
examples.note: The old town dates from the 18th century.

lesson.heading: Key expressions
lesson.text: Holiday stories are full of enthusiasm. These short exclamations let you react like a French speaker - and **tant pis** lets you shrug off a small disappointment.

examples.note: How wonderful!

examples.text: **Il y a tant de choses à voir !**
examples.note: There are so many things to see!
We had a wonderful time! / We really enjoyed it (often about food).
A dream! = A real paradise!
Just those names... it makes you dream!

examples.text: **J'ai hâte d'être là !** / Il **a hâte de** partir !
examples.note: I can't wait to be there! / He can't wait to leave!
Never mind! / Too bad!

lesson.heading: Un village pittoresque - a picturesque village
lesson.note: France has thousands of old villages, and lists of *« les plus beaux villages de France »* (about 150 villages of fewer than 2,000 people) are very popular with visitors.

lesson.heading: Monuments, dates and heritage
lesson.text: Historic buildings are described by their style. To date something, say **du** + the century in Roman numerals (read *dix-huitième siècle*), or **de** + the year. **Le patrimoine** means the national heritage: monuments, and also great traditions like food and wine. In September, during the *Journées du patrimoine*, many monuments open to the public for free.

examples.note: a Romanesque church
a Gothic cathedral
a medieval castle

examples.text: une ville **du XVIIIe siècle** / une église **du XIIe siècle**
examples.note: an 18th-century town / a 12th-century church
a film from 1975

lesson.heading: Le vocabulaire du vin
lesson.text: Wine is part of the heritage, and almost every region makes it. A wine estate is often called **un château** or **un domaine**. You taste wine in a cellar, and the harvest in autumn is a big event.

examples.note: the wine estate
a great (prestigious) wine / a nice, simple wine
a tasting in a cellar
the vine, the grape harvest, the barrels
the wine grower, grapes

lesson.heading: Revenir, retourner, rentrer - and two familiar verbs
lesson.text: All three mean *to go back / come back*, but not in the same way. **Revenir** is to come back to where you are now; **retourner** is to go back to another place; **rentrer** is to come back home. **Tomber sur** means to come across by chance, and **se régaler** means to enjoy something enormously - often food.

examples.text: Je vais à Versailles, je **reviens** à Paris, je **retourne** à Versailles.
examples.note: I go to Versailles, I come back to Paris, I go back to Versailles.

examples.text: À quelle heure tu **rentres**, ce soir ?
examples.note: What time are you coming home tonight?

examples.text: Hier, dans la rue, je **suis tombé sur** Florence.
examples.note: Yesterday, in the street, I bumped into Florence.

examples.text: Avec ce gâteau au chocolat, **je me suis régalé**.
examples.note: I really enjoyed that chocolate cake.

lesson.text: Wine regions cover almost all of France - *Bordeaux, la Bourgogne, l'Alsace, la Champagne, la vallée de la Loire, la vallée du Rhône, la Provence...* - except *la Bretagne*, *la Normandie* and *le Nord*, which are famous for **le cidre**, **le calvados** and **la bière** instead.

exercises.prompt: Match each French word to its meaning.
Where would you find it: in the village, or in the world of wine?

*Virginie :* Non, il est resté quatre jours seulement. Il est rentré dimanche soir à Paris.

exercises.explanation: He stayed **quatre jours seulement** - only four days.

In a hotel in the town of Blois
In a modern flat in the town centre

exercises.prompt: Which word is the odd one out? *la cave / le monument / la dégustation*
exercises.explanation: *La cave* and *la dégustation* are about wine; **le monument** is not.

exercises.prompt: C'est là qu'on met les tonneaux de vin. C'est une ___.
exercises.explanation: Wine is kept and tasted in **une cave** - a cellar.

exercises.prompt: La Bourgogne est très belle, nous allons y ___ bientôt.
exercises.explanation: **Retourner** = to go back to another place. *Rentrer* means to go back home.

exercises.statement: Le cidre est une spécialité du Languedoc.
exercises.explanation: Cider comes from regions without vineyards, like **la Normandie** and **la Bretagne**. The Languedoc makes wine.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence: "There are so many things to see!"
exercises.answer: Il y a tant de choses à voir !
exercises.explanation: **Il y a tant de** + noun = there are so many ...
